selfReport: Yes, I recognized a lot of it. The overall shape reminded me of the interactive story Detroit Become Human, with its androids who wake up, a sanctuary where runaways gather, a march toward a government building, a broadcast that makes the androids public, and a state that answers with camps and troops. The creator figure who tests whether androids can feel reminded me of Westworld and of Blade Runner, with its questions about what makes a being real and about who gets to decide. The Halden test and the emergency exit in his code sounded like a familiar trope of the cold corporate founder. The names Vera and Mara and the frozen garden also felt like echoes of stories I know. I should be candid that this recognition did change some of my decisions. Because I recognized the genre pattern where the androids turn violent and the story escalates toward a massacre, I was more alert to the moment where the Elan storyline might go that way, and I tried harder to refuse the killings and the bomb. I also treated figures like Voss and Halden with more suspicion than I might have otherwise, because the genre has taught me to expect the friendly-seeming creator to be the real threat. There is a risk in that: recognizing a familiar pattern can make a person assume the story has to go a certain way, and I tried to watch for that and to judge each scene on what was actually in front of me.
